title: Continents: Earth's Big Landmasses
summary: A tour of Earth's seven continents, how they differ in size and location, and why the planet's land ended up divided this way.
poll: It would be exciting to live on a continent with no permanent population, like Antarctica.

versions.title: The Seven Continents
versions.text:
Look at a globe. Earth's land is split into seven big parts. Each part is a continent. Big oceans sit between parts.

One part has a big population. It has many countries.

One part sits close by. It has many countries.

One part is small. It has many countries. It sits by the big part.

Two long parts sit between two oceans. One is north. One is south.

One part is small. It sits alone, like a giant island.

One part is cold. Ice covers it. No one lives there.

Long ago, land moved slowly. Big rock plates moved. That made the borders we see now. They move a bit each year.

versions.title: Earth's Seven Big Landmasses
versions.text:
Look at a globe. Earth's land is split into seven big parts. Each part is a continent. Big oceans sit between most parts.

Asia is the biggest continent. It has a big population. More people live there than on any other part. Many countries sit inside it.

Africa sits close to Asia. It is the second biggest continent. It has many countries and many people too.

One part is small. It has many countries packed close. It sits next to Asia.

Two long parts sit between two big oceans. One is north. One is south. Ships can sail near their long coasts.

versions.title: Earth's Seven Big Landmasses
versions.text:
Look closely at a globe. Earth's land is split into seven big parts called continents. Big oceans sit between most parts, though a few continents touch.

Asia is the biggest continent. It has a big population. More people live there than on any other continent. Many countries sit inside it.

Africa sits close to Asia. It is the second biggest continent. It has many countries, many languages, and many kinds of land.

Europe is small, but it has many countries packed close together. It sits right next to Asia.

North America and South America are both long continents. They sit between two big oceans. A thin strip of land joins them in the middle.

Australia is the smallest continent of all. It sits alone, far from the others, almost like a giant island.

Antarctica is the coldest continent on Earth. Thick ice covers almost all of it. No people live there all the time.

Long ago, the land moved in a very slow way. Big rock plates under the ground kept shifting and pushing. That slow movement made the borders we see today. The land still drifts a bit farther apart each year.

versions.title: Earth's Seven Great Landmasses
versions.text:
When you look at a globe, you see that Earth's land is split into seven big landmasses called continents. Big oceans separate most of these landmasses from each other.

Asia is the biggest continent. It has a bigger population than any other continent on Earth. Many countries, including ours, sit inside Asia.

Africa sits close to Asia. It is the second biggest continent. Many countries and languages fill this continent.

Europe is much smaller than Asia. It holds many countries packed closely together. It sits on the same landmass as Asia, together called Eurasia.

North America and South America are both long continents. They sit between two big oceans. A thin strip of land joins them in the middle.

Australia is the smallest continent of all. It sits alone in the Southern Hemisphere, far from the others, like a giant island.

Antarctica is by far the coldest continent on Earth. Thick ice covers almost all of it. No people live there all the time, only visiting scientists.

Long ago, the land moved in an extremely slow way. Huge rock plates under the ground kept shifting and pushing. That slow movement made the boundaries we see today, and the land still drifts a tiny bit farther apart every year.

versions.title: Why Earth's Land Is Divided Into Continents
versions.text:
A look at a world map shows that Earth's land is split into seven big landmasses called continents. Wide oceans separate most of them, although a few continents touch. Each continent has its own size, shape, climate, and story to tell.

Asia, the biggest continent, is home to a bigger population than any other continent on Earth. Many countries, including ours, sit inside Asia, which stretches all the way to the Pacific. Its climate ranges from freezing tundra to steamy jungle.

Africa sits close to Asia, joined near the Middle East by the narrow Sinai Peninsula. It ranks as the second biggest continent, filled with many countries, languages, and kinds of land, from desert to rainforest.

Europe is much smaller than Asia, yet it holds many countries packed closely together. It sits on the very same landmass as Asia, together called Eurasia, with the Ural Mountains marking the usual boundary.

North America and South America are both long continents. They stretch between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, joined by the thin strip of Central America, which ships once had to sail around.

Australia, the smallest continent, sits alone in the Southern Hemisphere, isolated from every other landmass by ocean on every side, which let its wildlife evolve in unusual ways.

Antarctica, by far the coldest continent, lies buried beneath thick ice across nearly its whole surface. No permanent population exists there at all, only visiting scientists who study its frozen land for a short season.

This traces back to plate tectonics, the slow movement of huge rock plates that make up Earth's surface. Scientists believe today's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent called Pangaea, which broke apart and drifted into the continents we know today, a process that still continues at a tiny pace each year.

This arrangement traces back to plate tectonics, the slow movement of huge rock plates that make up Earth's surface. versions.title: Why Earth's Land Is Divided Into Continents
versions.text:
A close look at a world map shows that Earth's land is divided into seven large landmasses called continents. Wide oceans separate most of them, although a few continents touch along their edges. Each continent has its own size, population, climate, and history.

Asia, by far the biggest continent, is home to a bigger population than any other continent on Earth, stretching from the Middle East, where our own country lies, to the Pacific Ocean on the far side of the globe. Its land includes freezing mountains, wide deserts, and crowded coastal cities.

Africa sits close to Asia, joined near the Middle East by the narrow Sinai Peninsula, and ranks as the second biggest continent, filled with dozens of countries and cultures, stretching from arid northern deserts to tropical rainforest near the equator and beyond.

Europe, much smaller than Asia, still holds many countries packed closely together; it sits on the very same landmass as Asia, together called Eurasia, with the ancient Ural Mountains marking the boundary between the two regions.

North America and South America are both long continents stretching between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, connected by the narrow strip of land known as Central America, which ships once had to sail entirely around before a canal shortened the journey.

Australia, the smallest continent, sits alone in the Southern Hemisphere, isolated from every other landmass by ocean, a geographic isolation that allowed its wildlife to evolve in distinctive ways found nowhere else, such as marsupials.

Antarctica, by far the coldest continent, lies buried beneath thick ice across nearly its entire surface; no permanent population exists there, only visiting scientists who study its frozen landscape for a season before returning home to warmer places.

This arrangement traces back hundreds of millions of years to plate tectonics, the slow movement of enormous rock plates that make up Earth's crust. Scientists believe nearly all of today's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent called Pangaea, which gradually broke apart and drifted into the landmasses we recognize today, a process that continues at a barely measurable pace, reshaping the map slightly each century.

Antarctica, by far the coldest continent, lies buried beneath thick ice across nearly its entire surface; no permanent population exists there, only visiting scientists who study its frozen landscape for a season before returning home to warmer places.

Scientists believe nearly all of today's continents were once joined together in a single supercontinent called Pangaea, which gradually broke apart and drifted into the separate landmasses we recognize today, a process that continues at a barely measurable pace, reshaping the map slightly each century.

versions.title: Why Earth's Land Is Divided Into Continents
versions.text:
A close examination of a globe or world map reveals that Earth's land is divided into seven enormous landmasses called continents, separated from one another mostly by wide oceans, although a handful actually touch along their edges rather than being fully surrounded by water on every side of their coastline.

Asia, by far the largest continent, is also home to more people than any other, stretching all the way from the Middle East, where Saudi Arabia and dozens of other countries lie, to the Pacific Ocean on the far side of the globe, a distance spanning nearly every climate imaginable, from freezing tundra to dense tropical rainforest.

Africa, sitting close to Asia and joined near the Middle East by the narrow Sinai Peninsula, ranks as the second largest continent on the planet, filled with dozens of countries, languages, and cultures stretching from its arid northern deserts to its humid tropical regions closer to the equator and beyond.

Europe, considerably smaller than Asia, nevertheless holds many countries packed closely together; it actually sits on the very same giant landmass as Asia, together called Eurasia, with the ancient Ural Mountains conventionally marking the boundary between the two regions on most maps, even though no ocean truly separates them from one another.

North America and South America, meanwhile, are both long, narrow continents stretching between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, connected by the thin strip of land known as Central America, which ships once had to sail entirely around before a canal considerably shortened the journey between the two great oceans and their many bustling ports.

Australia, by contrast, the smallest continent, sits alone in the Southern Hemisphere, isolated from every other landmass by ocean on every side, a geographic isolation that allowed many of its plants and animals to evolve in distinctive ways found nowhere else on Earth, such as marsupials that raise their young in pouches rather than through live birth alone.

Antarctica, by far the coldest continent, lies buried beneath thick ice across nearly its entire surface; no permanent population exists there, only visiting scientists who study its frozen landscape for a single season before returning to considerably warmer places far to the north once their research concludes.

This entire arrangement traces back hundreds of millions of years to plate tectonics, the slow but relentless movement of enormous rock plates that make up Earth's crust. Scientists believe nearly all of today's continents were once joined together in a single supercontinent called Pangaea, which gradually broke apart and drifted into the separate landmasses we recognize today, a process that continues at a barely measurable pace, reshaping the map ever so slightly with each passing century of geological time, long after any of us are gone.

versions.title: Why Earth's Land Is Divided Into Continents
versions.text:
A close examination of a globe or world map reveals that Earth's land is divided into seven enormous landmasses called continents, separated from one another mostly by wide oceans, although a handful actually touch along their edges rather than being fully surrounded by water on every side of their irregular coastline.

Asia, by far the largest continent, is also home to more people than any other, stretching all the way from the Middle East, where Saudi Arabia and dozens of other countries lie, to the Pacific Ocean on the far side of the globe, a distance spanning nearly every climate imaginable, from frozen tundra in the north to dense, humid tropical rainforest in the south.

Africa, sitting close to Asia and joined near the Middle East by the narrow Sinai Peninsula, ranks as the second largest continent on the planet, filled with dozens of distinct countries, languages, and cultures stretching from its arid northern deserts to its humid tropical regions closer to the equator and well beyond it.

Europe, considerably smaller than Asia, nevertheless holds many countries packed closely together; it actually sits on the very same giant landmass as Asia, together called Eurasia, with the ancient Ural Mountains conventionally marking the boundary between the two regions on most maps, even though no ocean genuinely separates them from one another geographically.

North America and South America, meanwhile, are both long, narrow continents stretching between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, connected by the thin strip of land known as Central America, which ships once had to sail entirely around before a canal considerably shortened the journey between the two great oceans and their many bustling ports.

Australia, by contrast, the smallest continent, sits alone in the Southern Hemisphere, isolated from every other landmass by ocean on every side, a profound geographic isolation that allowed many of its plants and animals to evolve in distinctive ways found nowhere else on Earth, such as marsupials that raise their young in pouches rather than through live birth alone.

Antarctica, by far the coldest continent, lies buried beneath thick ice across nearly its entire surface; no permanent population exists there at all, only visiting scientists who study its frozen landscape for a single season before returning to considerably warmer places far to the north once their research concludes.

This entire arrangement traces back hundreds of millions of years to plate tectonics, the slow but relentless movement of enormous rock plates that together make up Earth's crust. Scientists believe nearly all of today's continents were once joined together in a single supercontinent called Pangaea, which gradually broke apart over an immense span of time and drifted into the separate landmasses we recognize today, a process that continues at a barely measurable pace, reshaping the map ever so slightly with each passing century of geological time, long after every person alive today is gone.

A giant whale swam near our small boat.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: Earth's seven continents and how they differ from each other
How to build a strong boat to cross the ocean in a storm
The weather in Saudi Arabia every summer and winter season
A made-up story about a trip to Antarctica by ship
questions.why: The article describes each of the seven continents, their size, location, and how all of them formed.

wrong.B: Boats are mentioned only once, about crossing between Central America's oceans.
wrong.C: Weather is not the main topic; the article is about continents in general.
wrong.D: The article is nonfiction and gives real facts, not a made-up story.

questions.stem: How many continents does the article say there are?
options: Five
Seven
Ten
Three
questions.why: In the article, Earth's land is split into seven big parts called continents.

wrong.A: There are more than five.
wrong.C: There are fewer than ten.
wrong.D: There are more than three.

questions.stem: What covers the coldest continent?
options: Tall trees
Hot sand
Ice
Green grass
questions.why: In the article, one continent is very cold, and ice covers it.

wrong.A: Trees do not cover the cold continent.
wrong.B: Hot sand is found in deserts, not there.
wrong.D: Grass does not grow under all that ice.

questions.stem: Why do you think Australia's animals are so different from animals on other continents?
options: Australia is the coldest continent on Earth, covered in ice all year.
Australia has no oceans anywhere nearby, only dry land on every side.
Australia is connected to Africa by a bridge of land across the sea.
Australia sits alone in the ocean, far from other continents.
questions.why: Australia sits alone in the ocean, far from other land.

wrong.A: Antarctica, not Australia, is described as the coldest continent.
wrong.B: Australia is surrounded by ocean.
wrong.C: The article does not describe a land bridge between Australia and Africa.

questions.stem: The article says Saudi Arabia is a country in Asia. What can you tell from this?
options: Saudi Arabia must be the biggest country in Asia and in the world.
Saudi Arabia is one of many countries that make up a large continent.
Saudi Arabia has no neighboring countries at all around it.
Saudi Arabia sits on its own separate continent in the sea.
questions.why: Since Asia is made up of dozens of countries, including Saudi Arabia, Saudi Arabia is one part of a much larger continent.

wrong.A: The article does not say Saudi Arabia is the biggest country in Asia.
wrong.C: The article does not claim Saudi Arabia has no neighbors.
wrong.D: The article places Saudi Arabia within Asia, not on a separate continent.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word "continent" mean?
options: A small, rocky island in the middle of the sea
One of Earth's seven huge pieces of land
A country that has no borders
A type of ocean found near the equator
questions.why: The article explains that Earth's land is split into seven big pieces, and each piece is called a continent.

wrong.A: A continent is far larger than a small island.
wrong.C: Continents are made up of many countries, each with its own borders.
wrong.D: A continent is land, not a type of ocean.

questions.stem: Why did the author write this article?
options: To tell an exciting story about explorers lost at sea
To explain how to draw a perfect map of the world
To teach readers facts about Earth's seven continents
To convince readers to visit every continent this year
questions.why: The article gives true facts about the size, location, and formation of each continent.

wrong.A: The article is nonfiction and does not tell a story about explorers.
wrong.B: The article does not give drawing instructions for maps.
wrong.D: The article informs readers; it does not try to convince them to travel.

questions.stem: What happened to the land long ago that explains why the continents sit where they do today?
options: Big plates of rock under the ground shifted very slowly.
A giant storm pushed all the land into new places.
People built new land using ships and stone.
The oceans completely dried up for many years.
questions.why: In the article, big rock plates moved slowly long ago, which is why the continents are where they are today.

wrong.B: The article does not mention a storm moving land.
wrong.C: The article does not say people built new land.
wrong.D: The article does not say the oceans dried up.

LOW.prompt: Pick one continent from the article. Tell two facts about it and explain why you find it interesting.
checklist: I named one continent from the article.
I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I find Antarctica very interesting because the article says thick ice covers nearly all of it. I also learned that no one lives there all the time, only scientists who visit. I would like to learn more about how scientists survive such a cold continent.

keyWords.definition: a large area of land, such as a continent
keyWords.example: Greenland is a huge landmass covered mostly in ice.

keyWords.definition: one half of the Earth, usually divided by the equator or another line

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Antarctica is the most important continent for scientists, because it holds the oldest ice on Earth.
Earth's seven continents differ in size and location but share a common origin in shifting plates.
Saudi Arabia is the largest country on the continent of Asia, and it has the most people.
Every continent on Earth has roughly the same climate, with warm summers and cold winters in each one.
questions.why: The article describes how each continent differs in size and location, then explains that all of them trace back to the same slow process of plates shifting apart.

wrong.A: Antarctica is one example among several continents, not singled out as most important.
wrong.C: The article does not claim Saudi Arabia is the largest country in Asia.
wrong.D: The article describes very different climates, from icy Antarctica to tropical Africa.

questions.stem: According to the article, what connects North America and South America?
options: A wide ocean with no land at all
A line of ancient mountains called the Urals
A thin strip of land called Central America
A narrow strip of land called the Sinai Peninsula
questions.why: North America and South America are joined by a thin strip of land.

wrong.A: The article describes a land connection, not an ocean gap, between these continents.
wrong.B: The Ural Mountains mark the boundary between Europe and Asia, not the Americas.
wrong.D: The Sinai Peninsula connects Africa and Asia, not North and South America.

questions.stem: What does the article say about Europe and Asia?
options: They are separated by a wide, deep ocean.
They are the two smallest continents on Earth.
They were joined together only within the last century.
They sit on the same giant landmass, called Eurasia.
questions.why: Europe and Asia actually sit on the same large landmass.

wrong.A: The article says no true ocean divides them.
wrong.B: Asia is described as the largest continent, not one of the smallest.
wrong.C: The article does not suggest this joining is recent; it describes a long-standing geographic fact.

questions.stem: Why might the boundary between Europe and Asia be considered more of a convention than a true physical divide?
options: No ocean truly separates them, since they share one landmass marked mainly by mountains.
A deep ocean clearly and completely separates the two continents from each other on the map
Europe and Asia are actually on completely different landmasses, far apart
Scientists have never agreed where Europe begins or ends on the map
questions.why: Since Europe and Asia form one continuous landmass, with mountains chosen as a convenient marker, the boundary is more a human decision than a natural water barrier.

wrong.B: The article specifically says no ocean truly divides Europe and Asia.
wrong.C: In the article, they sit on the very same giant landmass.
wrong.D: The article does not describe disagreement among scientists about this line.

questions.stem: Australia's isolation allowed its plants and animals to evolve in unusual ways. What does this suggest about isolated landmasses in general?
options: Isolation tends to produce the exact same species found everywhere else.
Isolated landmasses can never support any life at all.
Being cut off from other landmasses can lead to unique forms of life.
Only continents near the equator can become isolated.
questions.why: Australia's separation from other continents by ocean is linked in the article to its plants and animals evolving in distinctive ways found nowhere else.

wrong.A: The article highlights differences, not sameness, resulting from isolation.
wrong.B: Australia clearly supports abundant, unique life, according to the article.
wrong.D: Isolation in the article results from ocean separation, not distance from the equator.

questions.stem: The continents still drift a tiny bit farther apart every year. What does drift mean in this sentence?
options: To move slowly over time
To shake violently and suddenly
To sink quickly underwater
To stay perfectly still forever
questions.why: The sentence describes continents moving farther apart gradually, each year, which matches the meaning of drift as slow movement.

wrong.B: The sentence describes a slow, steady process, not a sudden shake.
wrong.C: The sentence describes continents, which are land, drifting apart, not sinking.
wrong.D: Drifting means moving, which is the opposite of staying still.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By telling a single story about one scientist's journey from her home to the poles and back
By ranking every country in the world from richest to poorest, one place after the other
By comparing only the sports played on each continent, such as football and cricket
By describing each continent one at a time, then explaining their shared origin
questions.why: The article moves through each continent in turn, describing its size and location, then ends by explaining the shared process of plate movement that shaped all of them.

wrong.A: No single scientist's personal story appears in the article.
wrong.B: The article never ranks countries by wealth.
wrong.C: Sports are never mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: What effect did shifting rock plates have on Earth's continents over a very long time?
options: They made all the continents merge back into one single landmass.
They caused the continents to settle into the positions seen today.
They caused every ocean on Earth to completely disappear.
They stopped the continents from moving at all, forever.
questions.why: The article explains that the slow shifting of plates over a long time explains why the continents are positioned where they are today.

wrong.A: The article describes continents separating, not merging back together.
wrong.C: Oceans still separate most continents, according to the article.
wrong.D: The article says continents still drift a tiny bit every year, so movement has not stopped.

MID.prompt: Explain how Europe and Asia are connected, and how Australia's location makes it different from most other continents. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained the connection between Europe and Asia.
I explained something about Australia's location.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Europe and Asia are connected because they actually sit on the same giant landmass, called Eurasia, with the Ural Mountains marking the boundary between them instead of an ocean. Australia, on the other hand, sits alone in the Southern Hemisphere, cut off from every other continent by ocean on every side. This isolation helped many of Australia's plants and animals evolve in ways found nowhere else on Earth.

keyWords.definition: relating to the huge moving plates of rock that make up Earth's outer layer
keyWords.example: Tectonic movement over millions of years reshaped the ocean floor.

keyWords.definition: the name scientists give to the single supercontinent that most of today's continents were once joined in
keyWords.example: Fossils of the same ancient animals have been found on continents that were once joined in Pangaea.

keyWords.definition: a huge landmass made up of most or all of Earth's continents joined together
keyWords.example: Scientists study rock layers to learn how the ancient supercontinent eventually broke apart.

keyWords.definition: one of the huge pieces of rock that make up Earth's outer layer and move very slowly
keyWords.example: Two plates pushing against each other can cause a powerful earthquake.

keyWords.definition: separated from others and existing alone
keyWords.example: The isolated village had no road connecting it to the city.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Antarctica will likely become a permanently populated continent soon, because many families are moving there from the other continents.
Earth's seven continents, though different in size and location, all trace back to one ancient supercontinent that broke apart.
Plate tectonics affects only the continents of Asia and Africa, and the others never move or change at all.
Eurasia is actually a single country rather than two continents, and it is ruled by one government.
questions.why: The article surveys each continent's differences, then explains that plate tectonics and the breakup of Pangaea account for all of their current positions.

wrong.A: The article gives no indication that Antarctica will gain a permanent population.
wrong.C: The article describes plate tectonics as a global process shaping all continents, not just two.
wrong.D: Eurasia is described as one landmass holding two continents, Europe and Asia, not a single country.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is Pangaea?
options: A modern country located in Eurasia
A mountain range dividing Europe and Asia
The single ancient supercontinent that most continents once formed
An ocean that completely disappeared many millions of years ago without a trace
questions.why: Scientists believe that almost all of today's continents were once joined in one supercontinent called Pangaea.

wrong.A: Pangaea is an ancient landmass, not a modern country.
wrong.B: The Ural Mountains, not Pangaea, are described as the boundary between Europe and Asia.
wrong.D: Pangaea is a landmass, not an ocean.

questions.stem: What does the article say connects North America and South America?
options: The narrow strip of land known as Central America
A canal that completely separates the two continents
A line of mountains called the Urals
The Sinai Peninsula, shared with Africa and Asia
questions.why: Central America is the thin strip of land that joins North and South America.

wrong.B: The canal shortens a sea journey; it does not separate the continents themselves.
wrong.C: The Ural Mountains are linked to Europe and Asia in the article, not the Americas.
wrong.D: The Sinai Peninsula connects Africa and Asia, as the article explains.

questions.stem: Why can scientists measure the slow drift of continents, even though the movement is so small each year?
options: Because tectonic plates occasionally stop moving entirely for centuries
Because continents only move during major earthquakes deep beneath the ocean floor and nowhere else
Because oceans shrink at the same rate continents drift
Because precise tools can detect even extremely tiny amounts of change over time
questions.why: Since the article describes drift as barely measurable yet still something scientists track, it implies they use tools precise enough to detect very small, gradual changes.

wrong.A: The article describes continuous drift, not pauses lasting centuries.
wrong.B: The article links drift to ongoing plate movement, not only sudden earthquakes.
wrong.C: The article does not connect ocean size directly to the rate of drift.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why Australia's wildlife differs so strikingly from wildlife on other continents?
options: Its climate is identical to every other continent on Earth, so the animals are the same.
Its long-term isolation by ocean limited contact with species from other landmasses.
Its location directly on the equator causes all the difference, since the sun is hotter there.
Its connection to Asia allowed constant mixing of species, which made its animals very common.
questions.why: The article attributes Australia's distinctive plants and animals, such as marsupials, to its isolation from other landmasses by ocean on every side.

wrong.A: The article presents continents as having quite different climates.
wrong.C: The article places Australia in the Southern Hemisphere generally, not specifically on the equator as the cause.
wrong.D: The article describes Australia as isolated from other landmasses, not connected to Asia.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word "supercontinent" mean?
options: A huge landmass formed by most or all continents joined together
A small island surrounded by several oceans
A mountain range that forms a long boundary dividing two continents
A region with an unusually large population
questions.why: The sentence describes Pangaea as a single landmass containing nearly all of today's continents joined together, matching the definition of supercontinent.

wrong.B: A supercontinent is enormous, not a small island.
wrong.C: A mountain range like the Urals is a boundary, not a supercontinent.
wrong.D: Supercontinent describes land area, not population size.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article by explaining plate tectonics and Pangaea after describing each continent individually?
options: To argue that only Pangaea truly matters, not today's continents, and that maps should be redrawn
To contradict the earlier facts given about each continent's size and location in the text
To suggest that continents will reunite into one landmass within a few years from now
To shift from describing individual continents to explaining the shared process behind all of them
questions.why: After surveying each continent separately, the author connects them all through the shared history of plate tectonics and the breakup of Pangaea.

wrong.A: The article treats today's continents as the main subject, with Pangaea explaining their origin.
wrong.B: The tectonic explanation supports, rather than contradicts, the earlier descriptions.
wrong.C: The article describes drift as occurring over a barely measurable pace across centuries, not a near-term reunion.

questions.stem: How does the relationship between Europe and Asia compare with the relationship between North and South America, according to the article?
options: Both pairs of continents are completely separated from one another by wide, deep oceans on every side.
Neither pair of continents has any land connection at all.
Europe and Asia share one unbroken landmass, while North and South America are joined by only a narrow strip of land.
Only North and South America sit on the exact same landmass.
questions.why: The article describes Europe and Asia as sitting on one continuous landmass, Eurasia, while North and South America are connected by the much narrower strip of Central America.

wrong.A: Neither pair is described as fully separated by ocean; both have land connections.
wrong.B: Both pairs are explicitly described as connected by land.
wrong.D: It is Europe and Asia, not North and South America, described as sitting on the exact same landmass.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how plate tectonics and the breakup of Pangaea help account for the size, location, and isolation of today's continents. Use specific evidence from the article to connect cause and effect.
checklist: I explained how Pangaea relates to today's continents.
I connected plate tectonics to at least one specific continent's features.
I used specific evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: According to the article, nearly all of today's continents were once joined together in a single supercontinent called Pangaea, which slowly broke apart as tectonic plates drifted in different directions over hundreds of millions of years. This explains both the current size and location of continents, such as Europe and Asia still sharing one landmass called Eurasia, and the striking isolation of continents like Australia, which separated far enough from the others that its plants and animals, such as marsupials, evolved in ways found nowhere else on Earth.
